scenes.heading: Polymers
scenes.sub: Giant molecules built from thousands of small units
scenes.say: Plastic bottles, non-stick pans, water pipes and clothing fibres are all polymers. How can chemists make them soft, stiff or heat-proof?

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Party guests grab the next person's shoulder to form a conga line
scenes.science: Each C=C bond opens up to link monomers into a polymer chain
scenes.breaks: real chains have thousands of units, tangle together, and the 'hands' are really pairs of electrons.
scenes.say: Picture party guests, each with both hands on their own hips. That's a monomer with a double bond. To start a conga line, each person lets go with one hand and grabs the next person. One bond of the double bond opens up and links to the next monomer. Nobody's left out, so addition polymerisation makes no other product.

scenes.heading: Addition polymerisation
scenes.say: Here's ethene turning into polyethene. n ethene monomers join to make one long chain. The bit in brackets is the repeating unit.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: A polymer is –CH₂–CHCl–CH₂–CHCl–. Find the repeating unit and the monomer.
lines: Put the double bond back: CH₂=CHCl
scenes.say: This polymer repeats every two carbons, so the repeating unit is C H two, C H C l. Take two carbons and put the double bond back. The monomer is chloroethene, and the polymer is P V C.
scenes.caption: This polymer repeats every two carbons, so the repeating unit is –CH₂–CHCl–. Take two carbons and put the double bond back: CH₂=CHCl. The monomer is chloroethene, and the polymer is PVC.

scenes.heading: LDPE vs HDPE
scenes.say: Low density polyethene has lots of branches, like Christmas trees that can't stack closely. So the forces between chains are weaker, and it's soft and flexible. High density polyethene has straight chains, like planks, that pack tightly. Stronger forces make it stiffer and stronger.

scenes.heading: Heating plastics
scenes.say: A thermoplastic is like chocolate: heat it and it softens, so it can be remoulded and recycled. A thermoset is like toast: heat it more and it just chars, because covalent cross-links lock the chains together.

scenes.heading: Plastics and sustainability
points: Most plastics come from fossil fuels
scenes.say: Most plastics come from fossil fuels. Bioplastics use renewable feedstocks, but be careful: bio-based doesn't mean biodegradable. Polyethene made from sugarcane is identical to the fossil fuel version. Recycling can be mechanical, by remelting, or chemical, back to monomers.

points: Polymers: long chains of monomer units
scenes.say: Quick recap. Polymers are long chains of monomers. In addition polymerisation the double bond opens and nothing else forms. Condensation polymerisation releases a small molecule, usually water. Branching and cross-links control the properties. Now try the practice questions!
